question: What is the main goal of food and nutrition when caring for a patient receiving palliative care?

options.B: Building muscle mass and healing wounds
options.C: Extending life by forcing high calorie intake
options.D: Promoting comfort and quality of life

explanation: Great job thinking about holistic care! In palliative care, we focus on what brings the patient peace and enjoyment rather than trying to reverse the disease or force weight gain. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T17#GNS321_U4_T17_h1)

question: Why can forcing large meals cause problems for a patient with an advanced illness?

options.A: It causes physical distress like nausea and cramping
options.B: It instantly cures the loss of appetite
options.C: It interferes with daily physical therapy
options.D: It speeds up the metabolism too quickly

explanation: Spot on! When the body is weak, its digestive system slows down. Heavy meals just lead to discomfort like belly pain and nausea, rather than good nutrition. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T17#GNS321_U4_T17_h1)

question: What does the term 'cachexia' mean in advanced illness?

options.A: A sudden increase in daily appetite
options.B: Complete blockage of the large intestine
options.C: An infection caused by poor dental hygiene
options.D: Severe muscle wasting and weight loss

explanation: You've got this! Cachexia is a whole-body wasting condition caused by disease inflammation, not just because the person isn't eating enough food. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T17#GNS321_U4_T17_h2)

question: A patient says they feel completely full after eating just two spoonfuls of porridge. What is likely happening?

options.A: Rapid healing of the stomach lining
options.B: An allergic reaction to the specific ingredients
options.C: A sudden surge in physical metabolism
options.D: Early satiety caused by slowed digestive function

explanation: Exactly! When digestion slows down in advanced illness, the stomach fills up extremely fast—a concept we call 'early satiety'. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T17#GNS321_U4_T17_h2)

question: When is the best time to give antiemetic (anti-nausea) medication to a palliative patient who struggles with nausea at meal times?

options.B: Only when the patient falls asleep
options.C: Right after finishing a large plate

explanation: Well reasoned! Giving the anti-nausea medicine ahead of time stops nausea before it starts, helping the patient actually enjoy a few bites of food. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T17#GNS321_U4_T17_h3)

question: A patient with terminal cancer feels too tired to finish three standard meals a day. What is the best nursing action?

options.C: Switching entirely to thick liquid supplements
options.D: Forcing them to finish the plate before resting

explanation: Brilliant choice! Breaking food down into tiny, easy-to-manage snacks saves their energy and prevents them from feeling overwhelmed. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T17#GNS321_U4_T17_h3)

question: What is the main purpose of 'comfort feeding' in palliative care?

options.A: Maximizing pleasure and honoring patient preferences
options.B: Lowering blood pressure through low-salt choices

explanation: Spot on! Comfort feeding means throwing out strict diet rules so the patient can simply enjoy their favorite tastes and feel happy. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T17#GNS321_U4_T17_h4)

question: Why might a nurse relax a patient's long-standing diabetic diet restrictions during palliative care?

options.A: Sugar has no effect on blood glucose in terminal patients
options.B: Strict dietary control is no longer relevant to their comfort and quality of life
options.C: Diabetes automatically cures itself in advanced illness
options.D: Patients with terminal illnesses can no longer taste sweetness

explanation: You nailed it! Chronic disease rules are meant for long-term health. In palliative care, bringing a smile with a sweet treat matters much more. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T17#GNS321_U4_T17_h4)

question: What is a common physical risk of giving artificial IV hydration to a terminal patient?

options.A: Instant relief from all body pain
options.C: Rapid weight gain in muscle tissue

explanation: Correct! Because failing organs cannot process extra fluids well, IV drips can cause painful swelling and chest congestion instead of helping. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T17#GNS321_U4_T17_h5)

question: Why do family members often feel so distressed when a dying patient stops eating?

options.A: They are worried about the cost of purchasing groceries
options.B: They know that eating is the only cure for their illness
options.C: They believe the hospital kitchen is refusing to cook
options.D: They may view food as a symbol of care and worry the patient is being neglected

explanation: Very true. In our cultures, feeding someone is a deep act of love, so seeing them refuse food can feel heartbreaking to the family. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T17#GNS321_U4_T17_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a helpful way for families to show love when a patient stops eating?

options.A: Forcing the patient to swallow liquid supplements
options.B: Moistening dry lips with a swab

explanation: Great clinical instinct! Forcing supplements causes distress. Love is best shown through touch, wet swabs for dry lips, and quiet presence. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T17#GNS321_U4_T17_h6)

question: Why is it important to educate family members about natural nutritional decline at the end of life?

options.A: To prove that the medical team is working hard
options.B: To relieve their guilt and help them understand the dying process
options.C: To train them to insert feeding tubes at home
options.D: To prepare them to cook large meals for staff

explanation: Spot on! Teaching families that refusing food is a normal part of the body shutting down helps lift their guilt and brings them peace. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T17#GNS321_U4_T17_h6)
